instagram.caption: The ghost at Callahan House? Alice Callahan, the first person in Longmont to own and drive a car. Her husband had zero interest in learning, always used a chauffeur. Meanwhile Alice had her own ride and drove it herself, sometime around 1905. Full episode with Elizabeth Beaudoin in bio.

facebook.post: On this week's Longmont Locals episode, Elizabeth Beaudoin told us about Alice Callahan, the woman in white who's said to haunt the historic Callahan House downtown. Alice was a personality in early Longmont: she was the first person in town to own and drive a car, around 1905, likely a Stanley steamer. Her husband? He had no interest in learning to drive and always used a chauffeur. Alice had her own garage built out back and drove herself. The Callahans later gifted the house to the city in the 1930s as a meeting space, and it sounds like Alice never really left. What's your favorite piece of early Longmont history that doesn't get talked about enough?

instagram.caption: Ever wonder why every haunted house looks Victorian? Turns out there's actual history behind it. On this week's Longmont Locals episode with Elizabeth Beaudoin, we dig into why those ornate homes became spooky shorthand when they fell into disrepair mid-century. Full episode link in bio.

facebook.post: Why does every haunted house in movies look like a crumbling Victorian mansion? There's real architectural history behind it. On this week's Longmont Locals, Elizabeth Beaudoin walks us through how Victorian homes went from symbols of wealth to icons of decay in the mid-20th century, just as Hitchcock and others were defining what 'scary' looked like on screen. Increased taxes on the rich, the shift to modernism, and a whole generation literally haunted by their parents' aesthetic. It's a fascinating little thread connecting architecture, economics, and pop culture. What's your favorite example of a spooky Victorian in a movie or show?

bluesky.post: Victorian homes became the haunted house archetype because they were literally falling apart mid-century when scary movies took off. A whole generation haunted by their parents' taste.

facebook.post: In the 1920s, the Shy family ran a clothing store on Main Street. One day they received a threatening letter on official KKK letterhead—leave town or else. When the story hit the newspapers, the Klan's response was to claim someone must have stolen their stationery. It wasn't them, they insisted. Except, of course, it totally was. On this week's Longmont Locals episode, Elizabeth Beaudoin walks us through this piece of our town's history, including the fact that Colorado had the second-highest Klan membership in the country during that era. What other stories from 1920s Longmont do you wish more people knew about?
